passage:
Monday. Keya had spent the weekend on her first market report. Asif glanced through it at his desk, phone pressed to his ear, and slid it back. "Redo this. Tighter." Then he turned away to his call.
Tuesday. She rewrote the summary four times, not sure what 'tighter' meant. Was it the numbers? The length? Every time Asif walked past, she opened her mouth to ask and closed it again. At lunch Karthik, the other intern, said, "He's like that with everyone." She wasn't sure she believed him.
Thursday. She submitted the new version at 11 p.m., stomach tight, and lay awake wondering whether she'd already failed the internship, or whether Asif had simply had no time to explain.

qa.q: What one word did Asif use to say how Keya should redo the report?
qa.a: Tighter.

qa.q: Why did Keya keep opening her mouth to ask and then closing it?
qa.a: She was afraid asking would show she wasn't good enough 😰, and she couldn't tell if Asif was displeased or just busy.

qa.q: What small step could change things for Keya at this early stage?
qa.a: She could ask one specific question, like 'Is it the length or the numbers?', which is normal for an intern and would replace guessing with facts.

qa.q: What might Asif have been dealing with when he slid the report back?
qa.a: He was on a phone call and seemed rushed, so he may not have realised how little his one word explained or how it would land.

grounding: Over a week a woman intern told to redo a report with one word feels criticised, unsure if she failed or the senior is busy, and is afraid to ask.

passage: Aditi, you look exactly like I did at your age, staring at that email. Let your Zainab Aunty tell you something. I was twenty, an intern at a newspaper in Hyderabad. The chief sub-editor, Mr Reddy, pushed my first story back across the desk. 'Do it again.' Nothing else. I went to the washroom and cried, then rewrote it three times, guessing. Was my English bad? Did he think I was stupid? I was too scared to go and ask. Only months later did I learn he'd had four pages to close that night and barely read past my first line. So don't do what I did, beta. Go and ask your senior what was meant.

qa.q: What did Mr Reddy say when he pushed Zainab's first story back?
qa.a: He said, 'Do it again.' Nothing else.

qa.q: What was young Zainab afraid of as she rewrote the story three times?
qa.a: She feared her English was bad or that he thought she was stupid, and that fear kept her from simply asking.

qa.q: What advice does Zainab give Aditi, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To go and ask what the senior meant, because a busy senior's short words may have little to do with Aditi, and asking ends the guessing.

qa.q: What was that night like for Mr Reddy, as Zainab later learned?
qa.a: He had four pages to close and barely read past her first line, so his curt words came from pressure rather than judgement of her.

grounding: An aunt recalls being a young intern told to redo work without explanation, feeling criticised, unsure why, and too scared to ask.

passage:
You want to know about my first week at the agency? Okay. On Thursday I submitted my first market report. Two days of work, charts and everything. Harsha sir, the senior on my team, opened it, scrolled for maybe a minute, and said, "Redo this. By Monday." Then he went back to his calls.
That's it. No comments. No red marks.
I sat there with my face burning. Was it all wrong? Was it the format? Or was he just in a rush? I kept looking at his desk, trying to find a moment to ask, but every time I stood up my legs said no. I'm Pallavi, the new girl, and I spent the whole weekend redoing a report without knowing what was wrong with it.

qa.q: What did Harsha sir say after scrolling through the report?
qa.a: "Redo this. By Monday."

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she kept looking at his desk?
qa.a: She felt anxious and criticised, unsure whether she had failed or he was just busy, and too afraid to ask.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Pallavi at this early stage?
qa.a: Asking one short, specific question, such as which part to change first, before spending a weekend guessing.

qa.q: What might Harsha sir be experiencing in that moment?
qa.a: He may simply be rushed with calls and not realise how little his short instruction explained to a new intern.

grounding: Shows an intern told to redo a report without explanation, feeling criticised, unsure why, and afraid to ask.

passage:
Monday: Aparna handed in her first research summary at the NGO. Pankaj flipped through it, frowned, and said, "Needs to be redone. Tomorrow's fine." He was already dialling a donor.
Tuesday: Aparna stayed till eight, changing fonts, rewriting the introduction, adding charts she wasn't sure anyone wanted. Twice she walked towards his cabin and twice she walked back. What if the question showed she really didn't know anything?
Thursday: Pankaj glanced at the new version. "Better. The numbers section still needs sources." Aparna nodded, relieved and confused at once. Nobody had mentioned sources.

qa.q: What did Pankaj say the numbers section still needed?
qa.a: Sources.

qa.q: Why did Aparna walk back from Pankaj's cabin twice on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was afraid and anxious that asking would show she didn't know anything, so fear kept her from asking.

qa.q: What small step could have saved Aparna the long Tuesday evening?
qa.a: Asking Pankaj one clear question on Monday, such as what exactly needed changing.

qa.q: What is it like for Pankaj, busy with donors, when he hands back the summary?
qa.a: He is probably focused on his calls and assumes his short comment is clear, unaware how much guessing it causes.

grounding: Shows an intern asked to redo her work with little explanation, guessing for days because she is afraid to ask.

passage:
Avni, beta, sit. You're worried about your internship? Let me tell you about my first one, in 1998, at a newspaper.
I wrote my first piece on the water shortage. The senior editor, a gruff man called Mr D'Costa, read it standing up and handed it back. "Redo." One word.
I went to the canteen and cried into my tea. I was sure he thought I was useless. But I didn't ask him why. I was too scared.
So I rewrote everything, even the good parts. Three days later he said, "You've lost the best line. The first draft only needed a better opening."
Three days, beta. One question would have saved them. That's what I, your Sangeeta Masi, learnt.

qa.q: What was the one word Mr D'Costa said?
qa.a: "Redo."

qa.q: What was young Sangeeta feeling in the canteen?
qa.a: She felt hurt and scared, sure Mr D'Costa thought she was useless, and too afraid to ask him why.

qa.q: In the story, what choice could have changed how those three days went?
qa.a: Asking Mr D'Costa one question about what to fix, instead of rewriting everything, even the good parts.

qa.q: How might Mr D'Costa have seen the situation?
qa.a: He probably thought "Redo" was enough and didn't notice how frightening one word could be for a new intern.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling being told to redo her work with no explanation, feeling criticised and afraid to ask.

passage: "Redo this. Before six, please." Ishita dropped the printed report on Parveen's desk, two tables circled in red, and was already walking to the lift with her laptop bag, phone at her ear. It was 4:10. Parveen stared at the circles. Were the numbers wrong, or only the layout? The single note in the margin said "no". Her chest tightened. Three weeks into the internship, this was the first real task anyone had trusted her with. She opened a chat to Ishita, typed "Sorry, could you tell me what", then deleted it. Maybe Ishita was rushing to a meeting. Maybe she thought the whole thing was hopeless. The office printer jammed twice while Parveen reprinted the old draft, and the clock kept moving. She rebuilt both tables from scratch, guessing at every line.

qa.q: What time was the report due, and when did Ishita hand it back?
qa.a: It was due before six, and it was 4:10 when Ishita dropped the report on Parveen's desk.

qa.q: Why did Parveen delete the message she had started typing?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid to ask, unsure whether Ishita was just busy or thought the work was hopeless, so asking felt risky.

qa.q: What small step would help Parveen right now?
qa.a: She could send one short, specific question, such as whether the problem is the numbers or the layout, so she stops guessing.

qa.q: How might Ishita see this moment?
qa.a: Ishita may simply be rushing to a call and think the red circles are clear enough, not realising Parveen reads them as harsh criticism.

grounding: Shows an intern handed work back to redo with almost no explanation, feeling criticised, unsure of the reason and too scared to ask.
